elements.content:
• HTML is the foundation of the web

• Learning goal: build a basic web page

• Course structure and timing

actions.text: Good morning, everyone! I’m Dr. Maya Patel, and I’m excited to start our journey into web development. Today we’ll see why HTML is the foundation of every website and what we’ll achieve by the end of this course.

First, HTML—HyperText Markup Language—gives structure to web pages, kind of like the skeleton of a body. Without it, a browser would have nothing to display. Our learning goal for this session is to create a basic web page from scratch.

We’ll follow a clear structure: a brief lecture, hands‑on coding, and quick check‑ins. By the end of today’s class, you’ll have a simple page that includes headings, paragraphs, and links, and you’ll know where to go next in the course.

To keep us on track, we’ve allocated roughly 15 minutes for the overview, 30 minutes for the coding demo, and 15 minutes for practice and questions. Feel free to pause me at any point if something isn’t clear.
Let’s get started and build that foundation together!

elements.content:
• – declares HTML version

• <html> – root element

• <head> – meta info, includes <title>

• <body> – page content

elements.html: <!DOCTYPE html> <html> <head> <title>Page Title</title> </head> <body> Content goes here </body> </html>

actions.text: Good morning, everyone! I'm Dr. Maya Patel, and today we'll break down the basic structure that every HTML page must have.
First, notice these key parts listed here: the doctype declaration, the root <html> element, the <head> section with its <title>, and the <body> where all visible content lives.
Let's look at the actual code for the doctype. The line <!DOCTYPE html> tells the browser which version of HTML we're using, and it's the very first line in any HTML document.

Putting it all together, a minimal HTML page starts with the doctype, then opens the <html> tag, includes a <head> section for the title, and finally a <body> section where you place text, images, or other elements. That's the complete, required hierarchy for a valid HTML document.

elements.content:
• Heading hierarchy: <h1> … <h6>

• One <h1> per page

• Create paragraphs with <p>

• Page outline example

actions.text: Good morning everyone! I’m Dr. Maya Patel, and today we’re going to learn how to organize our web pages using headings and paragraphs. Understanding this structure will make our content clear and accessible.

First, let’s look at the heading hierarchy. HTML provides six levels of headings, from <h1> down to <h6>. Think of <h1> as the main title of the page, and the others as sub‑titles that break the content into sections.
A best practice is to use only one <h1> per page. This tells search engines and screen readers what the primary topic is, and it keeps the page’s structure logical.

For regular text blocks, we wrap them in

tags, which create paragraphs. Paragraph tags add spacing and make the text easier to read.
Finally, here’s a visual example of a simple page outline, showing how the headings nest and where the paragraphs fit. Use this pattern as a template for all your HTML pages.

elements.content:
• Hyperlink syntax: <a href="url">text</a>

• Open link in new tab: add target="_blank"

• Embed image: <img src="path" alt="description">

• Alt text improves accessibility

actions.text: Alright everyone, let's dive into Links and Images, two essential tools for adding navigation and visual content to our web pages.
First, the basic hyperlink syntax uses the anchor tag: text. This creates a clickable link that takes the user to the specified URL.
If you want the link to open in a new browser tab, you add the attribute target="_blank" to the anchor tag.
Next, to embed an image, we use the img tag: . The src attribute points to the image file, and alt provides alternative text.
That alt text is crucial for accessibility—it describes the image to screen readers and shows when the image can't load.
To recap, we've covered how to write hyperlinks, open them in new tabs, embed images, and why alt text matters. Any questions before we move on?

elements.content:
• Ordered list: <ol> with <li> items

• Unordered list: <ul> with <li> items

• Nested lists create hierarchy

• Choose ordered for sequence, unordered for grouping

actions.text: Alright everyone, let’s dive into lists in HTML. We’ll look at ordered and unordered lists and see when each is useful.
First, an ordered list uses the <ol> tag. Each item goes inside an <li> tag, and the browser automatically numbers them for us.
If you need a simple bullet list, you use <ul> with <li> items. The browser adds a disc or circle bullet before each line.
You can also nest lists—put another <ol> or <ul> inside an <li>—to show hierarchy, like steps within a larger process.
So remember: use ordered lists when the sequence matters, and unordered lists for items where order isn’t important. Any questions before we move on?

elements.content:
• Table container: <table>

• Rows and cells: <tr>, <th>, <td>

• Adding captions and headers

actions.text: Alright, let’s dive into tables – the way we organize data into rows and columns on a web page.
First, we need a <table> element, which acts as the container for everything. Inside it, each row is created with <tr>. Table headings use <th>, and regular cells use <td>.
Here’s a simple illustration: a table with two columns and three rows. Notice how the first row could serve as a header, and each cell lines up under its column.
You can also add a <caption> element above the table to give it a clear title, and use <th> elements to label each column, which helps screen readers and improves accessibility.
That’s the core of building a table – container, rows, cells, optional captions, and header cells. Any questions before we move on?

elements.content: Forms: Collecting User Input

• Form container: <form>

• Input types: text, email, submit

• Labels and accessibility

• <textarea> and <button> elements

<form>
<label for="name">Name:</label>
<input type="text" id="name" name="name">
<label for="email">Email:</label>
<input type="email" id="email" name="email">
<button type="submit">Send</button>
</form>

actions.text: Good morning, everyone! I'm Dr. Maya Patel, and today we're diving into the basics of building a web form—how we collect user input on a website.
First, every form starts with a <form> container. Inside it, we'll use different input types: text for names, email for addresses, and a submit button to send the data.
Notice the bullet that says "Form container: <form>"—that tag tells the browser this section is a form, and it groups all the fields together.

Now let's look at a simple example. Here we have a label linked to an input with the name attribute. The <label> tag improves accessibility because screen readers can read the label when a user focuses on the input field.
We also include a <textarea> for longer messages and a <button> element that works the same as a submit input but gives us more styling flexibility.

To recap, a basic contact form includes a <form> wrapper, various input types like text and email, proper labels for accessibility, and optional textarea and button elements for richer interaction. Any questions before we move on?

elements.content:
• Sectioning elements: <header>, <nav>, <main>, <section>, <article>, <footer>

• Improves accessibility for screen readers

• Boosts SEO by clarifying content hierarchy

• Replace generic <div> with meaningful tags

actions.text: Alright everyone, let’s dive into Semantic HTML and see how we can give our pages real meaning.
First, notice these sectioning elements: <header>, <nav>, <main>, <section>, <article>, and <footer>. Each of these tells browsers and assistive tools what part of the page they’re looking at.
Using semantic tags improves accessibility because screen readers can announce the structure, and it also helps search engines understand the content, boosting SEO.
Instead of filling everything with generic <div> tags, we replace them with meaningful tags that describe the role of each section—making our code easier to read and maintain.

Quick checklist: use a <header> for introductory content, <nav> for navigation links, <main> for the core topic, <section> for related groups, <article> for independent pieces, and finish with a <footer>.
That wraps up our look at semantic markup—remember, meaningful tags make our sites more accessible and easier for everyone to understand.

questions.question: Which HTML tag is used to create a level 2 heading?
questions.analysis: The <h2> tag defines a level‑2 heading. <heading2> is not a valid HTML tag, <title> is used in the head section for the page title, and <header> is a semantic container, not a heading level.

actions.text: Hi everyone! Let’s dive into a quick knowledge check on the HTML basics we just covered. Read each question carefully, and think about the reasons behind each answer.

First, remember that heading tags define the structure of a page. A level‑2 heading is created with the <h2> tag, which signals an important sub‑section under a main heading. It’s not <heading2> or <title>, which serve different purposes, and <header> is a container for introductory content rather than a heading itself.

Next, the element is a self‑closing tag that displays an image. It always needs an attribute to describe the image for screen readers, and it uses the src attribute to point to the image file. Because it’s self‑closing, you can’t place text or other elements inside it.

Finally, a semantic element tells the browser and developers what the content means.

actions.text: Alright, everyone, let's wrap up what we've learned and look ahead to where you can go next.

First, we reviewed the overall document structure—how HTML pages are built with elements like headings, paragraphs, lists, tables, forms, and links, and why using proper semantics matters for accessibility and SEO.
Remember, clean, readable HTML means consistent indentation, meaningful element names, and adding comments where helpful. That makes your code easier for both humans and browsers to understand.

For further practice, I recommend the MDN Web Docs for in‑depth reference, freeCodeCamp's interactive exercises, and the HTML5 tutorial series on YouTube. Those resources will reinforce what we've covered today.
Thanks for your attention today—keep experimenting with HTML, and feel free to reach out if you run into any questions. See you next time!
